title: What Is Better, and the Limits of Wisdom
summary: A string of proverbs tells what is better: a good name than perfume, mourning than feasting, patience than pride. The Teacher then observes that the righteous sometimes perish while the wicked live long, warns against extremes, and confesses that no one on earth is righteous without sin. He tried to be wise but found wisdom beyond reach, and his search yields only a few bitter findings, ending with this: God made people upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
story: Chapter 6 ended by asking who knows what is good for a person. Chapter 7 answers, in part, with a series of better sayings, the kind of practical wisdom found in Proverbs. But the Teacher does not simply hand down traditional wisdom. He tests it against what he has seen and finds that it does not explain everything: good people die young, bad people prosper, and wisdom itself cannot be fully grasped. This begins the second half of the book, where the theme shifts from what people gain to what people can know. The chapter moves from confident proverbs to an honest admission of failure, and that movement is the lesson.
historical: The chapter reflects the life of a wisdom teacher in a society with courts, bribes, servants, and inheritances. Verse 7 warns that extortion and bribery corrupt even the wise, a concern shared by Israel's law (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19) and by wisdom texts across the ancient Near East. Verse 10 warns against asking why the old days were better, a question that could be asked in any age, whether by those who looked back to David and Solomon or by those living under foreign rule after the exile. As elsewhere in the book, the details fit either a Solomonic setting or the later Persian or Greek period that many scholars prefer.
cultural:
Houses of mourning were a regular part of life. When someone died, relatives and neighbors gathered for days of lament, often joined by professional mourners (Jeremiah 9:17-18). The Teacher says it is better to go there than to a feast, because there a person is forced to face the truth that death is the end of everyone. Laughter, by contrast, is like the crackling of thorns under a pot (verse 6): dry thornbushes burned fast, loud, and hot, but gave little lasting heat. In Hebrew the saying is also a sound play, since the words for thorns and pot sound alike (sirim and sir).

Verse 1 is another play on sounds: good name (shem) is better than good oil or perfume (shemen). Perfumed oil was a luxury used at feasts and for anointing, and its fragrance was fleeting; a name, meaning a person's reputation and character, outlasted it. The passage about the woman who is a snare (verse 26) echoes Proverbs 5 to 7, where the adulteress or foreign woman leads young men to death, and Proverbs 9, where Folly is personified as a woman calling to the simple.
literary: Verses 1 to 12 are a collection of comparative proverbs built on the pattern better X than Y; the word good (tov) appears eleven times in the chapter. These sayings are not random: many deal with death, sorrow, endings, and patience, and together they commend a sober, clear-eyed way of life. Verses 13 and 14 draw the conclusion that God has made both good days and bad, and no one can straighten what he has bent. Verses 15 to 22 turn to the Teacher's personal observation and advice about righteousness, wickedness, and human sin. Verses 23 to 29 are a first-person report of a search that largely fails, dominated by the verb to find (matsa), which appears repeatedly: the Teacher sought but did not find. In verse 27 the narrator's voice briefly breaks in (says the Teacher), a reminder that the book is framed by a second speaker.

outline.t: Better the house of mourning than the house of feasting
Patience, the past, and wisdom as a shelter
Consider the work of God: good days and bad
The righteous perish and the wicked live long; avoid extremes
No one is righteous without sin
Wisdom beyond reach, and the little that was found

doctrines.note: “Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (7:20). The Teacher's observation matches the whole Bible's diagnosis. Verse 29 traces the problem to its root: God made humanity upright, and the corruption came from human scheming, not from God's design.

Wisdom is a shelter that preserves life (7:12) and makes the wise stronger than rulers (7:19). Yet the Teacher resolved to be wise and found it beyond him (7:23-24). Biblical wisdom includes knowing the limits of one's own understanding.

God has made the day of prosperity and the day of adversity alike, so that no one can predict what comes next (7:14). The Teacher does not say God causes evil; he says both kinds of days lie within God's ordering, which calls for joy in good times and reflection in hard ones.

words.note: Tov, good or better. It appears eleven times in this chapter, most often in the comparative form, better than. The Teacher is testing what is truly good for a person (the question of 6:12), and his answers overturn common expectations: mourning, sorrow, rebuke, and the day of death are, in some sense, better than their cheerful opposites, because they teach wisdom.

Matsa, to find or discover. It appears nine times, mostly in verses 24 to 29, and it carries the drama of the section. The Teacher searches, adding one thing to another, and mostly does not find. What he does find is sobering. The repetition makes the point that honest inquiry has limits, and that the result of a genuine search may be a clearer sense of what cannot be known.

Chokmah, wisdom. In the Old Testament it means skill for living, from the craftsman's skill to the ruler's discernment. In this chapter wisdom is praised as a shelter, an inheritance, and a strength, yet the Teacher confesses that full wisdom was beyond him. He holds both claims at once: wisdom is worth everything, and no one has all of it.

Tsaddiq, righteous. It describes a person whose life conforms to God's standard and who is faithful in relationships. Verse 15 notes that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness, verse 16 warns against being overly righteous, and verse 20 says no one is righteous without sin. Together the verses question any confidence that careful goodness guarantees a good outcome.

christ: Paul's summary of the human condition in Romans 3:10-23, that none is righteous and all have sinned, is drawn mainly from the Psalms (Psalms 14 and 53), but Ecclesiastes 7:20 says the same thing plainly, and the gospel begins from that confession. The Teacher sees that God made humanity upright and that people have gone their own way (7:29); the New Testament announces that God has acted in Christ to make people righteous by grace, not by the careful self-management that the Teacher found wanting. Christ is also called the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). The wisdom that was out of reach and very deep (7:24) has come near in a person. These are connections of theme and fulfillment, not predictions in the text. The chapter's preference for the house of mourning also finds an echo in Jesus's blessing on those who mourn (Matthew 5:4).

hard.q: What does the Teacher mean by the bitter woman in verse 26 and not finding one upright woman in a thousand (verse 28)?
hard.a: These verses are among the most troubling in the book, and interpreters read them in several ways. Some take them as the Teacher's honest but limited observation, the words of a man in an ancient patriarchal world, which Scripture records without endorsing, much as it records his other conclusions that the book later qualifies. Others argue that the woman who is a snare is not women in general but the seductive woman or Lady Folly of Proverbs 5 to 9, and that verse 26 is a warning against folly rather than against women. Some note that a thousand recalls Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:3), and read the verse as a comment on what that king found among his harem, not a judgment on womankind. Still others point to verse 29, which uses the general word for humanity (adam) and concludes that God made human beings upright and all have gone astray, so that the search found both sexes wanting. Many readers combine these observations. What is clear is that the chapter's final word indicts humanity as a whole, and the rest of Scripture honors women as fully bearing God's image (Genesis 1:27) and praises the woman of strength in Proverbs 31.

questions: Why might going to a funeral teach you more than going to a party? What have you learned in a house of mourning?
Verse 16 warns against being overly righteous. What might that look like, and how is it different from simply being good?
The Teacher admits that wisdom was beyond his reach. How does it feel to admit the limits of what you understand, and how can that admission be a form of wisdom?
